node.label: Transnational history
node.description: Historical approaches examining connections across political and social boundaries and the making of those boundaries. Selected interventions question national units, unequal circulation and the historical categories used to describe movement.
node.scope_note: Provisional separate teaching entry for an approach with multiple histories, not a unified school. Global, international, connected, borderlands, migration, mobility and diaspora histories overlap without being interchangeable. Earlier roots and regional traditions need further review.

strands.title: Transnational History
strands.focus: Saunier presents transnational history as a diverse approach organized around connections across borders, rather than a single national narrative. Source-specific assessment, not a definition of the whole field. Transnational history is an approach with several contexts, not a synonym for global, international or borderlands history.
strands.attribution_note: Description-supported lead retained; no new body reading or practitioner promotion.

strands.title: On Transnational and International History
strands.focus: The 2023 forum reassesses an established transnational approach, asking what emphasis on flows and movement may have obscured. Source-specific assessment, not a definition of the whole field. Transnational history is an approach with several contexts, not a synonym for global, international or borderlands history.
strands.attribution_note: Twelve credited forum authors. The opening is the only substantive passage checked; individual essays and author-specific arguments remain unread. Metadata credit is not collective assent.

strands.title: Methodological nationalism and beyond: nation-state building, migration and the social sciences
strands.focus: Wimmer and Glick Schiller question the treatment of nation, state and society as naturally coincident units of analysis. A jointly authored methodological critique of dominant social-science tendencies; it does not assert that every earlier historian used a national container. Wimmer and Glick Schiller argue that studying transnational communities can reproduce boundedness and obscure differences of class, gender and power. Selected pp. 324–325 only; transnational research is not automatically free from the assumptions it criticizes. No universal rejection of community research inferred.

strands.title: Global Migration and Regionalization, 1840–1940
strands.focus: McKeown argues that growing global integration of migration accompanied increasing regional segregation. Selected opening of the 2007 conference paper; the argument concerns historical migration systems, not a claim that borders disappeared. Statistical estimates have not been independently reproduced. McKeown challenges histories that make Atlantic migration the norm and treat Asian movement as inherently different or external to globalization. Selected pp. 2–7; preserve differences in coercion, routes and political intervention. Counts include repeated journeys and have gaps; they are not counts of unique migrants.

strands.title: Beyond the present, the nation, and Europe: Three different uses of history in reflexive migration studies
strands.focus: Reinecke and Löhr distinguish deep-history, genealogical and contrapuntal ways of relating past migration to the present. The coauthors’ analytical proposal, not a classification of all historians or an assertion that these modes began in 2024. Reinecke and Löhr propose using historical alternatives and ruptures to unsettle apparently inevitable categories of migration and belonging. Selected introduction and section 3; past alternatives do not erase enduring colonial inequalities. Their cited scholars’ works have not thereby been read independently.
